utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. There seem to be no preliminaries, which means that we go into closed session to hear the remainder of the testimony of the present witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. May I take it, Mr. Groome, that the Prosecution is ready to call Mr. Higgs after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we take a break, and we resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can deal briefly with a residual matter from the last witness. We have uploaded a corrected version of the document. It can be found in 65 ter 13858A, so at this time we would move that into evidence. The Chamber's already assigned the number, P2603.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 13858A is admitted into evidence, and appears under the number P2603 already reserved for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No need to have it under seal, Mr. Groome, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Higgs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Higgs. Mr. Higgs, you'll first be examined by Mr. Weber. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution and you'll find him to your right. Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, could you please introduce yourself to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Mr. Richard Higgs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you served in the British Army for 22 years from 1980 to the year 2002?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please give the Trial Chamber a general overview of your duties between 1987 and 2002.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: During that time I worked for a specialist branch within the army called the Small Arms School Corps, which specialises in technical weaponry and the training of those weapons. I started, first of all, using and training small arms weaponry, but then transferred across to dedicated mortar training, and then finished my time with the army as the senior technical expert for the British Army on mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 30280 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, is this the report that you completed for the Mladic case on the 8th of October, 2012.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On this first page of the report, you indicate that in the course of your duties you supervised the firing of over 14.000 rounds a year and conducting the firing of as many as 4.000 rounds in one day. Could you please explain to us the purpose of these firing exercises.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: These exercises spanned from small training exercises with individual mortar platoons in some cases, right up to a battalion, corps, and divisional level exercises in many countries around the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Throughout the remainder of this report, do you provide analysis concerning the general functioning of mortars in five particular shelling incidents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you personally visit the five locations discussed in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Have you testified before this Tribunal as an expert witness on three previous occasions in the Galic, Dragomir Milosevic, and Karadzic cases?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to review portions of your previous testimony from the Milosevic and Karadzic cases before today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the Milosevic case, did you provide additional testimony concerning your experience with mortar investigations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 30277, page 5, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, this is a transcript from your previous testimony in the Milosevic case. Directing your attention to line 14, do you have any corrections or clarification to your answer that begins, "When they can obtain ..."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's possibly due to translation, what that should say is "when they cannot obtain a direct line of sight."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are there any other corrections or clarifications to your previous testimony that you would like to make in either the Milosevic or Karadzic cases?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, is there any reason why you use a not official, not corrected version of the transcript, rather than an official one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can check into that. But ... if I could just have one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd be happy to look into it and I will get back to you as soon as I possibly can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions that you were asked during these previous testimonies, would you provide the same answers, in substance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution would tender five items. The Prosecution requests admission of the curriculum vitae for the witness under 65 ter 11036; the report of the witness under 65 ter 30280; portions of the previous testimony of the witness from the Milosevic case under 65 ter 30277; and the Karadzic case under 65 ter 30278; lastly, the Prosecution tenders one not admitted associated exhibit form the Karadzic case. It is an UNMO sitrep from 30 August 1995 after the Markale II incident under 65 ter 11190. And, Your Honour, in light of your inquiry, if the Milosevic testimony could remain marked for identification I'll check the official version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, let's take them one by one CV to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We object to those three report and to excerpts from the transcript in the line with our motion from 98th [sic] of August 2013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then the last one was the 11190.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar, we'll take them one. 11036, CV of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P2604. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. The next three will be marked for identification, both because a decision will be taken only after the end of the examination of the witness, but, also, as far as the Milosevic transcript is concerned because there is a -- in view of the version that has been used until now for which we will further -- we'll receive further information. 30280, the report will receive, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2605, MFI. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2605 is marked for identification. 30277, Milosevic excerpt of Milosevic transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be P2606. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2606 is marked for identification. Excerpts from the Karadzic testimony, 30278.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned P2607. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. Finally, 65 ter 11190.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P2608. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2608 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution requests leave to present a public summary of witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please read it for the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Richard Higgs provides expert evidence regarding the overall capabilities, operation and effects of mortars as well as the methods of determining the source and direction of mortar fire. The witness provides opinion, observations, and assessments of scheduled shelling incidents in Sarajevo, including the 1 June 1993 shelling of a football match in Dobrinja, G4; the 22 January 1994 shelling in the area of Alipasino Polje, G6; the 4 February 1994 shelling of a humanitarian distribution location in Dobrinja, G7; and both Markale I and Markale II. This concludes the summary of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. Could I ask clarification for something I really did not understand until now already. Mr. Higgs you said that your supervised the firing of over 14.000 rounds in a year, and you conducted the firing of as many as 4.000 rounds in one day. It came to my mind that after three and a half days you're done. Is that -- how could I -- how should I your testimony in this respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The two figures are not directly related in -- in the same year, Your Honour. It was just making the point that in some of the exercise I was supervising we were firing in excess of 4.000 rounds a day. And over a period of a year, in most years, in excess of 14.000 round. Some years would be more than that and some years would be less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So when you said and conducting the fire of as many as 4.000 rounds you were still talking about supervising them and that you had very busy days, but easy days as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. So I was responsible for all the firing that was taking place. That is not me personally firing a single mortar firing 4.000 rounds. That's me possibly supervising one or two or three battalions firing many mortars on the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Today, I like to beginning by discussing with you the purpose of mortars. On page 5.000 of your previous testimony in the Milosevic case, you state: "A mortar round is designed primarily to kill personnel. They are not destruct weapons, i.e., for blowing up large targets, buildings, and so on." In this respect, could you explain how mortars are designed to kill personnel.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The general design of a mortar round is one where the body of the round is manufactured in a way where it is maximised to fragment into small pieces, and therefore cause the maximum damage possible to personnel, infantry in the open. Mortar rounds break up into the smaller pieces; whereas your larger artillery rounds predominantly break up into large pieces of shrapnel. So that is the main difference between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You indicate that they are not destruct weapons. From a military perspective, would firing one or two mortars be an effective means of targeting buildings in urban areas where civilians are present?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: No, this wouldn't, for the reason I have already mentioned. Even with the larger mortars, i.e., the 120-millimetres, if you are trying to destruct a building then you would need to fire far more than just one or two rounds. It would require many, many, more rounds to get them the destruct capability that you're trying to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you were mixing up two things in your question, I think. You asked whether mortars be an effective means of targeting buildings in urban areas and then you added where civilians are present. Would it make any difference in the destructive power whether civilians are present or not? I mean, I did understand that it is a feature of the weapon which makes it unfit to destroy buildings so irrespective or whether there are -- who is around.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I was going ask another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It one would fire one to two rounds in an urban area where civilians were present, do you have any views of the intended purpose of such firings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: When firing mortar ammunition because you want to have the maximum effect when the round lands, if we were trying to neutralise a target, for instance, a larger military target, then we would fire far more than one or two rounds. We would normally concentrate our fire. So higher numbers, so then get maximum effect on the ground. The only time we fire small numbers of rounds is when we are trying to harass the target. So by firing small numbers into an area then prevents movement of people in that area. So firing small numbers rounds is more of a harassing-type mission than a killing or a destruction-type mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 3 of your report, you list the general type of available fuses. You indicate that air-burst fuses are for personnel in the open or for trenches without overhead cover. Could you please briefly explain to us how these fuses operate and what is their purpose.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: There are different types of air-burst fuses which can either work on a mechanical time-type fuse or on an electronic-type proximity fuse. And these are set then to detonate the round above ground level. So they'll detonate in the air above the troops, so that then the shrapnel from those rounds would then go downwards into the ground causing the maximum casualties possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do air-burst fuses leave any type of crater?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: No, these fuses will not leave a crater as they don't hit the ground. They will leave shrapnel marks on the ground, from where the shrapnel lands, but there will be no crater.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were air-burst fuses used in any of the incidents you reviewed for this case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Not on the cases I reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Another type of fuse you describe is a direct action fuse. Could you please explain how this type of fuse operates.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: This type of fuse detonates when it hits a surface, hence the word direct action. And the fuse on striking the ground will then detonate and some of these fuses also have the compatibility to be set on what is called a delay setting, which will cause the fuse to have a small delay before the round then detonates.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were direct action fuses used in any of the incidents you reviewed in this case and, if so, were you able to determine whether these fuses were set for an instantaneous or a delayed explosion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: It appears from the investigations that I carried out that on the cases that direct action fuses were used, and they were set on to their Super Quick function.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say "Super Quick" function what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Not delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What is the primary effect that is achieved by using such a fuse?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The primary effect is that this round will burst at ground level on contact with a surface, and due to the way the round is constructed, then, of course, the blast will go out sideways giving maximum effect of a single round. If it was set on delay, then the rounds would dig into the ground and therefore have less of -- the shrapnel would have less effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question. You said this round will burst at ground level if the ground is the first obstacle it finds on its way. Would it be above ground level if it hits a building or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. So it will detonate when it hits its first obstacle in its flight path, whether that be a roof of a building or the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If a direct action fuse is set for delayed explosion, would the crater pattern be different?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Because the ground -- the mortar round is now digging into the ground, the crater or the burst pattern is completely different because the round now is not above the ground level when it is detonating. It is now dug into the ground, so you get more of a deep crater as opposed to -- which you may see in some of your pictures like a flash where it has gone off at ground level. So you would expect to see a deeper hole in the ground if it has been set on to delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have P644, page 9 of the English original and page 8 of the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, while this next exhibit is coming up, I just want to let you know for the remainder of today I'm going to focus on some particular aspects of the individual shellings. I will start with the football match in Dobrinja on 1 June 1993, incident G4. The UNPROFOR crater analysis for this incident is now before you. Did you review this report by Captain Houdet as part of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the analysis for crater 1 and crater 2, the report indicates that the splinter patterns show that there is a minimum calibre of 81 millimetres. Do you agree with these conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, from when I visited the site and seeing the craters that were there, they resembled what I would call a medium mortar, i.e., one of 81- or 82-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to conclusion number 1, which states: "The distance between crater 1 and the roof of the buildings indicates a minimum angle of descent of 40.5 degrees." Is this consistent with your own personal observations of the minimum angle of descent between these craters and the buildings to the east?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In your report on this incident, you can conclude that: "The mortar rounds must have been fired from the Serb side of the confrontation lines." Could you please explain what you base this conclusion upon.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Looking at the pattern of the -- the craters in the ground, indicated an approximate angle that the mortar rounds would have struck the target, as they gave an indication that the mortar rounds did not arrive at an extremely low angle of descent and they did not arrive in an extremely high angle of descent. So they arrived in, what I would call, a common angle of descent, somewhere between the two extremities. Using this and then looking at range tables, either ranges, the mortars could achieve this sort of pattern, gives you ranges of 300 metres plus because a mortar could achieve that sort of angle with any of the charges available to it but with a minimum range of 300 metres. And in this case, the confrontation lines being so close, I think the estimation was only 200 to 250 metres away, would mean that to get that pattern on the ground the mortar would have to have fired from somewhere -- where the other side of the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution now please have P865, page 21 of the B/C/S version only.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, while this is being called up, I'm going to move on and discuss with you briefly the shelling on 22 January 1994 in the area of Alipasino Polje - this is incident G6 - where the children were sledding.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is a confidential document, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph from the BiH MUP investigation of this incident?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Based on this photograph, can you determine what calibre of mortar caused this crater?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: From the -- the picture we have, the crater seems to be very small, with minimal damage to the top of the surface, which would indicate it's more possible or likely to have been a medium mortar, i.e., around 82-millimetre calibre, rather than the 120-millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Would the pattern of this crater have been different if it was caused by a 120-millimetre round?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, has that question not been answered by the answer of the previous question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It has, but if the witness -- I'm just asking in case the witness has an opinion as to some different characteristics that would not have been present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would not have been different, of course, he could not have said that the pattern is most likely of a medium mortar, I mean, otherwise he would have said, I can't see the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness wants to add anything to his previous answer, he can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 9 of your report you state that the two 82-millimetre rounds "fell exactly as the mortar crew would have intended and will have caused maximum casualties among those trying to take cover." Could you please explain to us how you reached this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The two mortar rounds in this case here were fired in the -- the open -- the street in front of buildings with one round landing short time before the second and again with a dispersion -- a -- a distance apart. So to cause maximum casualties one way of doing this would be to fire one round, first of all, then knowing that people will move around in that area on finding out what is going on or running for cover and then fire the second round, of course, to make maximum use of that particular case. So that's how you would, in this case here, if that was the plan, by firing these two rounds at slightly distance apart with a shall time gap between them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'd like to move on and discuss with you the shelling of the humanitarian distribution line on 4 February 1994, incident G7. You make the observation on page 9 of your report that: "When I visited the scene, you become aware that the distances between these rounds falling is actually not very far. In all, a distance of approximately 40 metres radius from the first to the last rounds." What does the distance between these impacts indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Because these rounds are reasonably close together, it could indicate that it could have all been fired from a single mortar because the distances then between the rounds could quite easily be within the acceptable accuracy of a single mortar barrel firing all three rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You indicate in the report that these rounds were fired deliberately. This is a comment that you repeat also in other parts of your report. Could you please just generally explain to us what you mean by the term "deliberate"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: In firing of mortars, the word deliberate means that on firing a mortar that a charge has been selected, a bearing has then been placed onto the sight, then to allow the fire, of course, then to impact the ground where he intended to be. So that is what we call a deliberate fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, could I ask -- I take it that you always have to select the bearing. You can't fire a mortar without selecting a bearing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that is not true. You can fire mortars in different ways. You can fire a mortar by direct fire, first of all, if you happen to have a mortar that can see the target from the -- the mortar position. They can actually use their sight to engage directly and so they won't have to use an observer. So that is one method. The second method using an observer is where you have correct charges, bearings and elevations that you have set on the sight from information given to you from an observer. And in some cases it could be possible to fire a mortar just into an area where you are not putting any particular bearings onto the sight but to -- but just by pointing into an area and selecting a charge so that you would know that a round is going to land in just in a -- a large area but a known area, so you really can fire the mortar in three ways, so direct fire by using correct charge bearing and elevations or by just pointing into a general direction if that is the wishes of the persons who is firing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I must have misunderstood you. Because even if you do it by direct fire, then you're still determining a bearing where it should go, et cetera, but you do it in a different way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, you do it in a different way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the reason why I asked you this. Because is there any firing of a mortar which is not deliberate? That means you want to hit a target or an area or whatever, that's all always deliberate, opposite to firing at random or just not knowing what you're doing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you wasn't targeting a specific area, if for some reason you just wanted to fire a round into a general area for harassment or something like that, then you actually wouldn't have to put on precise bearings onto the mortar because purely from that work you could just point in the general direction, you know how far it is going to go per charge, and you could, if you wanted to, just fire a round into a general area. This, however, for reasons we've already mentioned would not be a very accurate way of firing the weapons system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But it still would be deliberately doing something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You would still - yes - be deliberately doing something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is not to clearly select an area but just to take a wide area or an approximate area which is still a decision-making process as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, I'm a bit puzzled by deliberate and non-deliberate firing, but I know do understand, more or less, what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I just have a few more incidents to discuss with you. Have you previously reviewed materials and analysed the shelling that occurred on 18 June 1995 at a water distribution point in the Simon Bulevar school located in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have P997, page 8 of the English original. Your Honours, the B/C/S translation of this, I see, is incomplete and I will be working of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any portion you would like to use, then you should briefly read it so that it will be translated for the accused. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, this is the UNMO daily sitrep dated 19 June 1995, a day after the shelling of the Simon Bulevar school. Directing your attention to the 7th entry from the top the one that states: "1146B," then in the next column, "OP-4," then, "one explosion or XPL," then the word, "unknown," then going across it states, "Dobrinja with a grid reference." And then in the column to the far right, it says, "fired BSA." Does the time of this entry correspond to when the shelling of the water collection point at the Simon Bulevar school occurred?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to the six-digit grid reference which for the record states B, as in boy, P865564 under the word Dobrinja, does this grid reference correspond to the approximate location where the shell impacted upon a wall of the school?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please move forward to page 12 of the English version of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, I had be drawing your attention to the section that states: "UNMO team SW-2 carried out investigation of 120-millimetre mor, origin approx 320 MAG. Difficult to confirm, fragments removed by local CIVPOL, and impact was on concrete wall 4 had M above ground level. The impact site was a water collection point. UNMOs were allowed to Kosovo hospital and the morgue where they could confirm 7 Civ killed." Do these findings of the UNMO investigation team with respect to that 320 MAG correspond to the findings of the BiH MUP related to this shelling?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Before asking you a few specific questions about Markale I on 5 February 1994, could you please explain to us the kinetic forces that are created when a mortar impacts upon a surface and explodes, both in terms of the shell which you've generally already explained and the stabiliser.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: When a round is striking the ground, it is obviously through the air at a specific velocity, and the velocity for this impact on the ground will depend upon the charge that it's been fired at. So the higher the charge, the faster the velocity, so the faster the round will impact the ground. When the round hits the ground and explodes, the force then will drive the -- the fuse part of the round into the ground which sometimes gives what is known as a fuse furrow or a hole in the ground where the fuse impacts itself into the ground. The round explodes, forcing the shrapnel out to the side because the rounds are designed for most of the blast to go sideways to cause the maximum casualties. And the tail-fin, of course, at the rear of the round is also travelling forward at the same speed as the round. So this has the same velocity as it's travelling forward as the round exploded, and so, therefore, again, at the higher velocities because it is moving forward with a higher kinetic energy which is why, as I explain in my earlier reports, is one of the reasons we tend to see tail-fins in some of the craters as opposed to not being in others because of the kinetic forces as round explodes and the velocity of the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect -- with respect to Markale I, do you have any views on the distance to which the mortar came from based on the depth of the stabiliser that was embedded into the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: In Markale I, the tail-fins were embedded deeply into the ground, which would tend to indicate that that particular round was fired on a higher charge rather than being fired on a low charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And when you say higher charge, what do you mean with respect to this incident?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: With respect to this incident and the type of ground, i.e., being a hard surface, the higher charges would be charges 5 and charge 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'd like to finish today with discussing briefly with you your evidence about Markale II. And, actually, since most of it is a part of your previous testimony, I'm going to show you just one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have P2055 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, did you review the still images and the video from which they come prior to today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Based on these images, do they appear to show the same stabiliser or a different stabiliser?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: From these two pictures, the damage caused to the tail-fins and the body of the tail-fin, they appear to be the same stabiliser.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are there any particular portions that are notable to you or particular observations that you have that correspond between those two photos?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: There is the -- the flattened nature of the tail-fins which appears in both. There is a polished upper surface to one of the tail-fins which you can see on both, and also to the bottom right-hand side corner of the main stem, you can see damage to the bottom right-hand corner which again appears on both.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. Mr. Lukic, is it you or is it Mr. Ivetic who will cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will cross-examine the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're pretty far away from the witness, and I have difficulties -- you are hidden more or less behind a pillar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will move forward, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You know this Chamber always wants everyone to move forward. If you would not mind that -- to move to a place where our communication is more direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would, Your Honour. I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, bear with us for a moment, so that Mr. Lukic is in full view. Mr. Higgs, you'll be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic, I think Mr. Mladic is seeking to consult with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one proposal. If we can make earlier break, since Mr. Mladic should leave the courtroom and he would waive his right to be present today and tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that is -- I'm looking at Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic, counsel tells us you would waive your right to attend the proceedings from after the break we are about to take up till and including tomorrow. Could you -- I take it that counsel has expressed your views on the matter? In that case, we would take an early break, and we would start cross-examination after the break. I see you're nodding yes in respect of everything I said the last minute. Yes. Then, Mr. Lukic -- could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then take the break, and we resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom, I'd like to inform the parties that, to the extent we'll need to sit in the first weeks of December, that we'll not sit on Wednesdays; so, therefore, the 4th of December, and the 11th of December, we would not sit. We do not know yet whether we use those days around these dates, but already to inform you that -- about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I put on the record that Mr. Mladic is not present in court. Before the break, he explicitly waived his right to attend the proceedings. Mr. Lukic, if you are ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Higgs.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will continue in B/C/S. I think you don't mind. I go swiftly in that way. [Interpretation] In your report, P2605, you say that: "It must be emphasised that I have been using evidence provided only by third parties and that I arrived at my conclusions based on the photographs of incidents and my experience with mortar incidents." Now, I'm going to start with Markale II of 28th August 1995, marked in the indictment as G18. In the report, you say that: "Based on the evidence presented to me, there is no reason for me not to trust the reports compiled by other organisations. They concluded that the bearing of the round made -- and the crater made by the round is 170 degrees."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly have 65 ter 10221.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is your report, as you can see, dated 3rd August, 2006. We need page 9 in B/C/S and page 10 in English. Under sub-item E, second paragraph you say: "I looked at all of these reports and by using data supplied, pictures of the scene and maps of the area, I was able to confirm the correct trajectory by using these methods." Do you stand by this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we get too confused of a record, I would just note that the same sentence appears in -- on page 13 of the witness's current report in this case, which is P2605.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With one exception. Not in the report, we can read bearings instead of tragedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, to the extent possible, please include the report which was prepared for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will discuss both reports, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, do you stand by this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that you have decided the bearing, the angle of ascent, the angle of descent, the trajectory, and the flight time of the projectile?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: There was nothing in the report to my recollection regarding the flight time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for the other elements, is it correct that you have defined them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. In my report, I looked at the evidence regarding the direction and the angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now briefly take a look at 65 ter 10233. This is a sketch indicating how the Sarajevo police determined the minimum angle of descent. You had an opportunity to review this document, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you check whether this angle of descent was correctly defined by them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. I had a look at this, the measurements taken, and agreed with their calculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, so we don't have too confused a record, this document is contained in Exhibit P00498.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's part of an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a large document, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can -- can we have the page in that document so it's clear for the record, please, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'd be happy to provide it. I'm just looking it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that if the angle of descent is less than 67 degrees, that shell would have hit a building or the building on the market?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, that would be correct. It would have hit somewhere on that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's briefly look at the direction from which the shell came or, rather, let's look at the way to establish the bearing of the pavement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, I would like to go back to 10221.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before moving on to the next document, for the record, what was on our screens is P498, page 24 in the B/C/S and page 22 in the original -- or in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now could the Court produce the sit-report from the 26th of August -- or, rather, the 3rd of August, 2006, and let's look at page 12 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you determined the direction by looking at the photo of the place of impact and the pattern on the asphalt, and, thus, you determined an approximate direction of the flight based on the way or the shape of the curb?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Using the information, I was trying to determine which direction the crater was facing, so I used the -- the picture and the line of the curb and the edge of the buildings to see if the crater was facing towards the buildings or, for instance, facing down the road so I could then try and ascertain which direction is -- was more likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Look at the figure "185 deg." What does that represent? It is degrees, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That angle just represents the right angle to the curb, the right-angle direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have received a somewhat odd interpretation. Is this the right angle, the normal angle of 90 degrees, with respect to the curb? We did not understand you in the interpretation, sir.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. 90 degrees to the curb, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The direction of the line, which is marked as 175 degrees, this is what you based on the pattern of the fragments on the asphalt, and that represents the direction from which the shell had come; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. I was looking at the general pattern of the crater and seeing in which kind of general direction it lines up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In that case, when you drew a line which is normal with respect to the curb, the 176, you looked whether the angle was to the left or to the right, with respect to that line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I took the line -- a general line which in this case the 275 is just a fixed point. It is not an accurate representation of the road. It's a fixed point that I then used as a reference point, as what I was trying to show in this diagram was the disparity between two reports, where we had a direction of 170 degrees and a direction of 220 and 240 degrees being suggested. So by using, then, this fixed line, I could then see which direction the mortar crater is facing which, in this case here, it is facing towards the building. Because if the crater had been fired from a direction more towards 220 or 240, then you'd expect to see the direction or the position of the crater facing more to the right down the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you use the same methodology in this case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: In this case -- I'm sorry, could you just explain the question? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What we are looking at is a photo from the Karadzic case, i.e., the report that you prepared for that case. Now have you been commissioned to do a report for the -- General Mladic case. Did you used the same methodology. This was my question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. In my report, I made the point that the bearing of 275 degrees here is not a representative bearing of exactly where the road faces. It was a fixed point that I could more accurately draw on a map at the time just to give me a rough direction to find out whether this crater was facing towards 170 or nearer to 220/240. Due to the fact that the -- the Karadzic case that did cause a little bit of confusion how I had done this, I, therefore, changed it for this particular case here to try and estimate the actual direction that the road faces along, and those bearings are in my up-to-date report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, I still have some difficulties in understanding what you meant exactly by: I took a fixed point. I mean, a line is not a point and it's apparently what you wanted with the 275 degrees. What you wanted to do is the -- establish the direction of the curb stones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. On the maps that I had at the time, and with the direction of the road, a little bit further on down the road here, we have a nice, really straight line which I could see on the map to give me a really clear direction, which was the 275, which I used in the Karadzic case, which is about -- I think it's is about 10 degree different from the true road. But it was close enough to -- for be able to just give an impression of, is this crater facing toward the building, or is it actually facing down the road, to find out whether it's nearer 170, or is it facing towards 220/240. So that's why I took that particular bearing at that time. But as you said, in the Karadzic case, it caused a little bit of confusion, so I then went back to the report and to a more accurate reading of this particular road and this particular point, that is the direction that is in my up-to-date report. I think I -- I haven't got the report in front of me, but I believe it is nearer -- 265 degrees is the true direction of the curb, as close as I could make it with the maps I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just assume that it is 265, although it says 260 in the present report --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that the difference is 15 degrees.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, with what seems to me to be the same line going through the heart of the crater which, in your previous report as we see it on our screens now, was 175 degrees, and now you say crater direction close to 170 degrees; whereas, if the curb stones move for 15 degree, I would expect the crater direction, which is just a calculation, to be -- to move 15 degrees as well and not just 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The calculation of the direction of the -- the mortar crater here, I am just obviously basing that on this picture and, of course, the findings of the examination team on the day, when they came up with that direction of being approximately 170. I have not used the angle of the curb or any mathematical calculation to then take one from the other. So I'm just using this picture just to represent that the crater is facing more towards an angle of 170 than it is to a direction of 220/240. I am not using this picture to accurately plot the exact direction of the crater because I don't have enough information to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on this photo, you estimated that the line that goes to the crater as -- slightly inclines to the left so the trajectory had to have been 170 degree, i.e., 10 degrees to the left; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I don't really understand the question. Could you just start again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on this photo, you estimated that the angle of the trajectory leans 10 degrees to the left, i.e., that it is 175 rather than 185, and 185 would have been a 90-degree angle with respect to the curb; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: In this case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we can therefore conclude that with respect to the curb, based on your findings, the projectile did not arrive at an angle of 90 degrees but, rather, at an angle of 100 degrees; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection. I don't think that's accurately stating the witness's evidence. If I could have a point where he might have referred that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you please explain how -- in the new picture, I see the direction of the curb to be 260 degrees. The crater direction close to 170 degrees, surprisingly, because I would expect even less, which makes a difference of 90 degrees rather than 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as we can see, the angle of the curb is marked here as 275 degrees. When you deduct 90 degrees from that, you arrive at 185 degrees. Using the same analogy, in order to arrive at an angle of decent of 175 degrees, you have to subtract 175 degrees from 275 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to follow you. You start with the Karadzic drawing. 275 degrees --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we see it on the right-hand side on this -- on this picture. 275 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the line of the curb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the line of the curb. And the line of the origin of fire is estimated, or, at least, is written down as 175 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which makes a difference of --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One hundred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of 100, yes. Now you want to compare that with what exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we have to come to the -- this -- the position of this curb, whether it's correctly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I now see your point. It's exactly the same point as you had pointed at before, that the -- if you change the angle slightly, then you would expect something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. Only we'll show it in more details, if you allow us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I would have similar concerns about the 220 degrees, as a matter of fact, but I have not raised that yet. I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you testified in the Radovan Karadzic case, it was established that you had erroneously calculated the bearing of the curb and that's why in your report dated 8 October 2011, you made a correction of that mistake; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question. He can ask that in a much more straightforward --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think the question is clear. Objection denied. What you intended to say, Mr. Lukic, is that the correct -- he now used the correct calculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He is trying to correct it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. He calculated it now according to his new views on the matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, do you accept that you made a mistake in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: No, I did not make a mistake. I was just using a different point of reference because I was not trying to directly ascertain the direction this crater was facing. I was just trying to work out whether or not it was nearer the 170, as put forward in one case, or nearer to 220/240, as put forward in another argument. So -- and from the picture, you can see that the crater is lined up facing the building and not pointing down the road. So this is not an accurate mathematical calculation on my behalf, just a guide to see which of the two reports I was faced with is actually the crater faces nearer towards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber would have to read the other report to see whether it was inaccurate because the drawing suggests otherwise, but without having read the report, we're unable to make any further conclusion, unless you take us through this alter report, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to tell you the position of our Defence, Mr. Higgs, and we will take it from there. It is our position that you intentionally calculated the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the -- Mr. Lukic please slow down. It is impossible to interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the position of our Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wanted to convey to you the message of the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- that if you would not slow down --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The message wouldn't be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That no message would come ever to our ears.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will repeat. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that I was reading too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Higgs, the position of our Defence is this: You intentionally miscalculated the bearing of the curb in order to arrive at an angle of 175 degrees because this is the bearing on which the Prosecutor located several positions from which the shell could have allegedly been fired. And now we are going to show you yet another excerpt from a map which you omitted from your report, although you did use it in your report that you drafted for the Radovan Karadzic case. We would like to call up 65 ter 100221. We are interested in the English page 13. Is this the map based on which you worked out the position of the curb?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: This is the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] On the left-hand side, we can see the angle of 275 degrees. And in order to increase the visibility we have enlarged one part so you will see that written within the map. Now I'm going to show you 1D1379. We can see the curb here and its position near the Markale market. You will see it marked as "Markale market." And we can see the direction of 275 degrees. This was plotted from your map, this line was plotted from your map onto this map. Is it true that in your first report, you used this map and this direction to establish the line of the curb in front of the Markale market and you arrived at a degree of 275 -- at an angle of 275 degrees?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, for the reasons I've already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you changed that because it confused some people. People were not confused. You made a mistake; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: No. I used the straighter line of road as it is further along to give me a line to work from, because I was only trying, as I said before, to work out or to disprove one bearing or the other whether it would be 170 or the angle of 220/240. Actually, by me using line 275 actually instead of helping or me trying to mislead, in some respects, it helps the Defence's case rather than the Prosecution's because now I have changed it to 265 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, Mr. Higgs, you don't have to explain whether it was favourable for the Defence or the Prosecution. First of all, we expected an expert --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to be accurate and not -- perhaps through mistakes, favour one of the two parties. Therefore, you would agree that if you plot on a photograph a direction in which a street runs, and if there's a considerable difference between the actual direction and the direction plotted, that that is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably a mistake in -- in interpretation but I was clear what I was trying to achieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs. Mr. Higgs, if I see a line plotted on a picture, which says whatever number, I expect that to be the real direction in which that street runs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other explanation needs more than what you are telling us. Because your purpose of what you are doing in itself does not allow for inaccuracy. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We checked or, rather, experts in the field checked the mistakes that you made on this occasion. And we measured the bearing of the -- city market on Google Earth, and the mistake was as much as 20 degrees. Do you now see as well that the error was 20 degrees?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The difference is approximately 15 degrees on my calculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And let's quickly look --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the end of our day. We will show more on this issue probably tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may do that tomorrow. But, Mr. Higgs, one final question. It's not only a matter of calculation. You calculate the difference between the two indicated on your maps, whether it's 275 or whether it's 260. How did you measure the 260?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 260, I then using this map here, to the best of my ability --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did it on the basis of this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this map, to the best of my ability, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you think that a cut-out of - how much is it? - just a couple of metres of 10, 15 metres would necessarily always be the same as what you find on a map with a totally different scale? Wouldn't you think that what you -- what we really need is to be with a compass at that specific point where the two bicycles are and measure it from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be the ideal way. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, because you said that you had visited the locations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did not do the measurements --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at that time. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No -- not any later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn for the day, Mr. Higgs. But before doing so, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak, communicate in whatever way, with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today, or whether that's testimony still to be given in the days -- in the coming days. You may follow the usher, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for the day. We'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 5th of November, at 9.30 in the morning, in this came courtroom, III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 5th day of November, 2013, at 9.30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.17 p.m.,
